findings.title: Blocked-email lookup can be bypassed by changing email case
findings.body: `should_block?` performs an exact database lookup using the supplied value, but signup assigns `params[:email]` directly to the user and does not normalize it. Consequently, a block for `blocked@example.com` does not match variants such as `Blocked@Example.com`, even though these are ordinarily delivered to the same mailbox and the rest of the domain restriction validation is case-insensitive. Normalize emails consistently when creating blocked records and when looking them up (and migrate existing entries) so the block cannot be evaded by case changes.

findings.title: Concurrent blocked-email checks lose match-count increments
findings.body: The code reads `match_count` into an ActiveRecord instance, increments it in Ruby, and saves it back. Two simultaneous validations of the same blocked address can both read the same count and overwrite each other, so `match_count` underreports attempted registrations. Use an atomic SQL increment/update (including `last_match_at`) or locking if these statistics are expected to be reliable under concurrent signup traffic.

findings.title: Email-change requests bypass blocked-email validation before sending mail
findings.body: The `change_email` action only checks whether the address is already in use, then creates an email token and queues an authorization email. It never assigns the address to the user or invokes the new `email` validator, so a blocked address can still be submitted through this endpoint and receives an authorization message. Validate the proposed normalized address here before creating the token/queueing mail; otherwise the blocked-email policy is not enforced for email changes (and may be bypassed entirely if token confirmation updates the email without validation).
